stories.title: Making Aja
stories.dek: How Steely Dan chased perfection in Los Angeles
stories.body:
By 1976, Steely Dan was no longer a band in the usual sense. Donald Fagen and Walter Becker, the duo at its core, had stopped touring two years earlier. They had decided that the studio, not the stage, was where their music could be made to sound exactly as they wanted. They hired the best session musicians in Los Angeles, and they recorded each song until it was just right.

Their sixth album, Aja, took shape in Los Angeles in 1977. The songs were more complex than anything they had tried. They mixed jazz harmony with rock rhythms, and they wrote parts for horns, strings and a rotating cast of musicians. Producer Gary Katz and engineer Roger Nichols helped Fagen and Becker chase the sounds in their heads. Players such as Steve Gadd, Chuck Rainey and Wayne Shorter turned up to record a single solo, and sometimes many takes were needed.

"Peg" shows how fussy the process could be. The duo wanted a lead guitar solo that was exactly right. Several top guitarists tried, and none of the solos satisfied them, until Jay Graydon recorded one that Fagen and Becker chose. The high background vocals on the song were sung by Michael McDonald, who by then was also the voice of the Doobie Brothers.

The title song, "Aja", ran close to eight minutes. It featured a long, dazzling drum part by Steve Gadd, who reportedly played it in just a few takes, and a saxophone solo by the jazz giant Wayne Shorter. Other songs, such as "Deacon Blues" and "Josie", told stories of disappointed dreamers and rowdy parties in Fagen and Becker's dry, knowing style.

The album came out in September 1977. It reached No. 3 on the US album chart and became the band's best-selling record, selling more than a million copies. It also won a Grammy for its engineering. Critics praised its sophistication, and later generations of jazz and rock musicians have studied it closely.

Aja is often put at the center of what some call yacht rock: slick, expertly played music with an effortless sheen. But Fagen and Becker's lyrics were sharper than the surface suggested. Behind the smooth grooves were characters who were lonely, scheming or lost. It was music made with great care, and it showed that polished pop could also be strange and very smart.

stories.title: What a Fool Believes
stories.dek: How Michael McDonald changed the Doobie Brothers
stories.body:
In the early 1970s the Doobie Brothers were a boogie band from the San Francisco Bay Area, known for the guitar-driven hit "Listen to the Music". The group was led by singer and guitarist Tom Johnston. In 1975, though, Johnston became seriously ill with stomach ulcers and could not tour. The band needed a replacement fast.

Guitarist Jeff "Skunk" Baxter, who had played with Steely Dan, suggested a keyboardist he knew who had sung backup for that group. His name was Michael McDonald, and he came from St. Louis, Missouri. He had a rich, soulful baritone, and he brought a feel for blue-eyed soul and jazz chords that was different from the band's usual sound. When he joined, the Doobies changed course. The album Takin' It to the Streets, in 1976, introduced the new direction, and after Johnston left in 1977, McDonald took over as the band's leader.

In 1978 the group recorded Minute by Minute. Its centerpiece was a song McDonald had been working on at his piano. He had a jaunty, rolling keyboard part and the start of a melody, but he did not yet have the words. His friend Kenny Loggins, a singer-songwriter who had enjoyed success with Loggins and Messina, came by. Loggins heard the riff and helped finish the lyrics, which told of a man clinging to the memory of a woman who has long since moved on. They called the song "What a Fool Believes".

It was a perfect meeting of two styles. The song had the sophistication of jazz and the instant hook of pop. McDonald's voice floated over a keyboard pattern that kept shifting, and the whole thing sounded polished and effortless. The Doobie Brothers released it as a single in early 1979, and it went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album Minute by Minute topped the album chart.

At the 1980 Grammy Awards, "What a Fool Believes" won both Record of the Year and Song of the Year, and the Doobies took home more awards that night. Loggins released his own version on the album Keep the Fire later that year.

The song has remained a favorite on the radio for decades. It helped define the sound that listeners later called yacht rock, and it made McDonald one of the most recognizable voices of the era.

stories.title: Toto IV
stories.body:
In the mid-1970s, a handful of young Los Angeles studio musicians were among the busiest players in the business. David Paich was a keyboardist and arranger. Jeff Porcaro, whose father Joe was also a respected drummer, played on hit after hit. They worked together on Boz Scaggs's 1976 album Silk Degrees, with bassist David Hungate, and the record's smooth sound became a template for what was to come. Paich and Porcaro began to think that they could make an album of their own.

In 1977 they formed a band called Toto with Hungate, Jeff's brother Steve Porcaro, guitarist Steve Lukather and singer Bobby Kimball. Their first album, in 1978, produced the hit "Hold the Line". But their greatest triumph came with their fourth, Toto IV, in 1982.

The album was recorded with great care, in the manner of the best studio work. It included "Rosanna", a song with a rolling shuffle rhythm that Jeff Porcaro built from the grooves of two other drummers. The title is often said to have been inspired by the actress Rosanna Arquette, who dated keyboardist Steve Porcaro at the time, though Paich has said the character was a composite of several women.

The other hit was "Africa". David Paich wrote it after watching a late-night television documentary about suffering on the continent, and he found himself imagining a place he had never visited. The track opens with a soft synthesizer and a shimmering percussion pattern, and builds to a soaring chorus, sung by the band as a group. Many of the songs on the record sounded effortless. In fact, every part was carefully planned, and the band used the best technical resources in Los Angeles.

The album was released in April 1982, and "Rosanna" reached the US Top 5. In February 1983, "Africa" rose to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. At the 1983 Grammy Awards, Toto won six trophies, including Album of the Year and Record of the Year for "Rosanna". For a group of studio players who had spent their careers backing other people, it was an astonishing victory.

Today "Africa" keeps finding new generations of listeners. The band proved that skilled session players could also write songs that captured the public imagination, and that polish and feeling could live in the same record.
